http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279225.text: Australia's sanctions aren't stopping Israel's settler funding Independent Australia 07 Aug 2026, 03:30 GMT+10 Despite three rounds of sanctions, Israel's financial support for the settler movement Australia targeted has continued to grow, writesWayne Hawkins. IN JULY 2024, Foreign Affairs MinisterPenny Wongannouncedsanctionson the Israeli settler networkHilltop Youthand seven of its members, citing beatings, sexual assault and torture of Palestinians. It wasn't a one-off. Australia has kept going: a second round in June 2025targetingIsraeli Finance MinisterBezalel Smotrichand National Security MinisterItamar Ben-Gvir, athird roundon 2 June 2026 adding three more individuals and four more entities including, for the first time, illegal farming outposts and ajoint statementon 9 June 2026 with the UK, Canada, France and Norway promising coordinated action against the networks that finance and enable settler violence. On paper, that looks like escalation. In practice,Al Jazeera reportsthe Israeli Government is now funding the same sanctioned movement to the tune of close to $40 million, on top of military protection and other state assistance. Three rounds of Australian sanctions, and the funding for the group they targeted has grown faster than the sanctions have. Despite diplomatic lobbying from the Israeli embassy, Labor delegates rejected efforts to dilute the party's stance on Gaza while shelving calls for stronger action against Israel. Part of the answer is structural and it's worth being precise about it rather than assuming bad faith. Hilltop Youth was never a registered organisation with a bank account to freeze it's a label for a loose, decentralised movement. When the U.S. Treasury sanctioned it in 2024, even theTimes of Israelnoted it was unclear the designation could be enforced, since there's no formal entity behind the name. Israel's stipend program follows that same seam: funds are paid to individual youths through regional councils, not to anything called Hilltop Youth. The sanctions were built for a movement; the payments go to people. But that only explains part of the $40 million. The harder case isHavat Gilad, a settler organisation that is explicitly under Western sanctions. Israel's National Security Ministry, run by Ben-Gvir, gave it $1.3 million anyway. Times of Israel reported it remains unclear whether that grant exposes the Israeli Government itself to secondary sanctions from the six Western governments involved.Peace Nowhas separately noted this is the first time Israel's government has funded the outposts this openly, while the responsible minister's office maintains the funding was coordinated with the Defence Ministry and lawful. So this isn't simply a loophole. In at least one case, it's money going straight to a named, sanctioned entity, with Israeli reporting itself asking whether that should trigger consequences nobody has yet imposed. In June 2026, Israel'sSettlement and National Missions Ministry, run byOrit Strook, confirmed a$1.9 million stipend program50 shekels (AU$23.45) a day, food vouchers, mediators for roughly 650 young settlers in illegal West Bank outposts, framed as violence prevention. Even then it was reported as a slice of a larger 120-million-shekel (AU$41.3 million) program. That larger figure is now confirmed, and theUN recorded over 1,330 settler attacksin the West Bank in just the first half of this year a period one of the movement's own leaders has described as a golden era. This isn't a fringe movement the Israeli State is failing to contain. Its founding call came from a foreign minister in 1998.Zvi Sukkot, a former Hilltop Youth figure, now chairs a Knesset committee. Ben-Gvir, the Minister whose ministry funded a sanctioned NGO, was himself convicted in 2007 of supporting a terrorist organisation and inciting violence. The movement Australia sanctioned has been substantially absorbed into the government we continue to treat as a full diplomatic and trading partner. The Royal Commission into Antisemitism has sparked debate over free speech, protest rights and the place of Palestinian perspectives in public discourse. None of this means Australia has done nothing; it means what Australia has done isn't landing. This is a structural problem, not a failure of any one minister or announcement: three escalating rounds of sanctions and the funding for the sanctioned movement has escalated faster than the sanctions could reach it. A commentary inMichael West Mediain June put it plainly, asking just how coordinated and effective these sanctions efforts have actually been, given settler violence has continued largely unopposed. A government can hold two positions that are formally consistent and practically hollow at the same time: we sanction this movement and we maintain full, unchanged diplomatic and trade relations with the state now funding it at record levels, including at least one payment to a name on our own sanctions list and call that a coherent Israel policy. It isn't. I've written before about resource sovereignty and about who actually holds power accountable to its stated commitments, locally in Tasmania and structurally in how governments behave when the mechanics of a policy stop matching its stated intent. This is the same pattern: a policy escalated on paper while the facts on the ground move faster in the opposite direction. Australians deserve sanctions that mean something. If ours do, our government owes the public an answer on how a movement it has sanctioned three times over is now better funded by Israel than at any point since those sanctions began and whether a payment to an entity already on our sanctions list changes anything. I've written to my local independent MP,Andrew Wilkie, asking that exact question be put on the record. It's a fair one to ask of every member of Parliament. Wayne Hawkinsis a small business owner in Hobart, Tasmania, and an independent candidate for the federal seat of Clark at the 2028 Election. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9qr.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, A major police operation has been mounted in Aarau, near Zurich By Rorey Bosotti Published 30 August 2026, 07:27 BST Updated 39 minutes ago A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting at a rave in Switzerland. The woman died at the scene in Aarau, police said. Those injured were four men and a woman aged between 24 and 27, all of whom are in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe". Organisers and performers confirmed the shooting happened at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in the town, which is located some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich. Police said the perpetrator's identity and possible motives were unknown, as were the "exact circumstances" of the incident. Local media reported that the force was alerted to the shooting around 02:30 local time (01:30 BST). A DJ who was due to perform until the scheduled end of the event at 02:00 said the incident occurred "straight after our set", in a post on social media. Another performer, DJ Tekibo, said he had lost a friend in the incident. He wrote on Instagram that he was "still trying to process what happened". Olivier Grein, whose firm Agency Events AG organised the event, said the company was "shaken" and would do all it could to support police. Organisers had expected up to 3,500 people to attend. Police asked witnesses to submit photographs and video from the scene. An area around the racing track, the town's swimming pool and sports field has been cordoned off, with the public urged to stay away. A large contingent of officers has also been deployed beyond Aarau "as a precaution", Aargau Cantonal Police said. An AFP journalist reported seeing armed officers deployed on the highway up to 30km (18 miles) from the site of the shooting. Aarau is located some 46km west of Zurich and is home to approximately 23,000 people. It is also less than 40km (25 miles) from the border with Germany. German media reported that police on the German side have been providing support to Swiss forces as the manhunt continues. Image source, EPA Image caption, Armed officers were deployed near the scene early on Sunday Images from Aarau early on Sunday showed a heavy police presence in the area, with an armoured vehicle seen blocking a road. Armed police and officers in riot gear could be seen patrolling the streets. In addition to police and fire officials, the regional disaster response unit (KKE) was deployed, according to broadcaster SRF. It also reported that a Swiss Army helicopter could be seen surveying the area in the early hours. Switzerland has one for the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years.
